name: Pioneer 9
payload: Solar-wind and interplanetary-field probe (65 kg per Siddiqi; NSSDCA lists 147 kg)
significance: Pioneer 9 was the last of four small, spinning NASA probes (Pioneers 6 to 9) sent into orbit around the Sun to sample the solar wind, magnetic fields and cosmic rays from widely separated points, so that scientists could watch the same solar storms sweep past different places in space. Pioneer 9 circled inside Earth's orbit, between 0.75 and 0.99 AU from the Sun. By May 1969 NASA reported that it had met all its goals and returned more than 6 billion bits of data, and it kept working for 14 years. Together the Pioneers turned the solar wind from a theory into something measured continuously, the first network of space-weather stations.
statusNote: Launched 1968-11-08 09:46:29 UT on a Thor-Delta E-1 from Cape Kennedy (Siddiqi). Solar orbit 0.75 x 0.99 AU, period 297.60 days, inclination 0.086 deg (NSSDCA trajectory record). NASA kept in contact until 1983-05-19; an attempt to reach it with SETI equipment on 1987-03-03 failed and it was declared inactive. TRAJECTORY (calculated, drawn dashed): JPL Horizons has no Pioneer 9 ephemeris and no measured trajectory is publicly archived, so the path is built from the published orbit (tools/build_solar_orbit_i.py): it starts at Earth's position at launch, where an inward-bound probe like Pioneer 9 is at its farthest from the Sun, and follows a two-body orbit with the published period until contact ended. The orbit's shape is right, but its exact orientation and the craft's place along it are approximate and drift over 14 years (planetary pulls are ignored), so the whole path is dashed. The 0.086 deg tilt is too small to see and is left out.
